{"category":"convention","enforced":false,"name":"A rule the project follows lives in the graph, not in an agent's memory file","statement":"Anthony, 2026-09-04, when offered a habit for the agent's memory: 'I prefer to add rules to the graph. If for instance I change development to another machine, I don't think memories are transferable. This is one of the reasons for reflow2.'

THE RULE: when a session learns something the PROJECT should keep — a working habit, a convention, a trap, a way of doing a step — it is recorded in the design graph, as a DesignRule, Decision or TemporalFact hung off the node it concerns. An agent's memory file may hold a POINTER to that node; it does not hold the content.

WHY, in three parts, all his:

① PORTABILITY. A memory file is machine-local and harness-local. The graph is a committed file that travels with the repository, so it resolves on any machine, for any agent, in any harness — `req:content-reaches-every-seat` states the same property for blob pointers and this extends it to governance. A rule only one seat can see is not a project rule.

② THE GRAPH IS THE PLACE THAT CAN ACT ON IT. A DesignRule can carry `enforced`, owe a detector, raise `unstated_rule_enforcement`, and be VIOLATED by a computation. A memory file can do none of those; it is prose an agent may or may not read. `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` is the case in point — it is enforced, it is in the graph, and it was still broken five times on 2026-09-04 by an agent whose memory held a paraphrase of it. The paraphrase reached nobody; the rule at least owes a check.

③ IT IS WHAT REFLOW2 IS FOR. His words: 'this is one of the reasons for reflow2'. A design brain that keeps its own operating rules somewhere it cannot read is the storyflow failure `dec:what-lives-where` describes — prose you navigate rather than a graph you query — applied to the tool's own conduct.

WHAT THE MEMORY FILE IS STILL FOR: who the user is, how they like to be spoken to, where things are on THIS machine, and pointers into the graph. Those are facts about a seat, not rules of a project, and a seat is exactly what a memory file is scoped to.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE: whether breaking it should stop the build. Nothing enforces where a session writes a lesson, and no detector could read a memory file it cannot see. `enforced` is deliberately left unstated here for the owner to rule on, per `dec:does-enforced-default-to-gate-blocking`."}
